doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

title: Race and the four white guys in the Basie band
summary: Sonny Payne's showmanship, then no racial friction in the band despite the history of segregation.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: such a showman and always stole the spotlight from whoever was up there. You know, throwing sticks around and doing all that. He’s one of my heroes, but I did hear those things, stories about him that was kind of like — talking about ego. You know? It probably got in the way there. So when I was on the band I was just trying to be — you know I was one of four white guys. There never was any racial indication from anyone on the band. From the top to the bottom. Nothing about black and white. No racial stuff, which was relaxing. Because those guys had gone through all that racial stuff. You know, staying in separate hotels and — one of the famous black bands and, “yeah you can come in and play the theater but you’ve got to leave out the back door and go to the other side of town and stay at the black hotel. You know, they’d been through all that. There was no —

No. There was no racial fighting at all. Four white guys. I was one of them. Eric Schneider was a tenor player from Chicago, Dale Carley was playing lead trumpet at the time, he’s from Silver Springs, Maryland, and Bob Summers was another trumpet player. We were the four white guys. There was never a black and white issue on the band, which made it so relaxed you know. Because there could have been very easily. You never know. Guys like Miles, he didn’t hide his racial preference. He told everybody, you know, crazy white men.
